metas.name: Catalonia - Catalan Language Tips
metas.note:
Sometimes described as a "mix" of Spanish/French, while not technically correct, can be a starting point to help identify Catalan. Spoken in the northeastern part of Spain called Catalonia along with the Valencian Community, Andorra, and the Balearic Islands. While you may see Spanish translations on signs there is a strong sense of independence in Catalonia and therefore often appears as the only language.

  • Uses "i" for "and" (unique to Catalan and the easiest identifier)
  • common endings = -tat -ció -ment (not unique but helpful)
  • look for tz, tx, tg, nyo(a) in words (some also used in Basque)
  • Word for "street" = carrer
  • Syllables and words ending in -aig, -eig, -oig, -uig, -aix, -eix, -oix, -uix
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: France - Basque Speaking France
metas.note:
Bilingual signs in Basque, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a thinner font, which is unique within all minority languages in France.

  • The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.
  • Basque is NOT a romance language but will almost always been seen in conjunction with French or Spanish. Basque is classified as a language isolate (unrelated to any other known languages) and the only language isolate in Europe.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: France - Corsican Language
metas.note:
On the French Island of Corsica you can find bilingual signs with corsican and French on it. There are also a few signs that only have corsica (if it's only French don't rule out Corsica as that is common as well).

The major language most closely related to corsican is italian. In particular, the endings u/iu/ju, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican.

Example in Corsican compared to Italian:

  • Sò natu in Corsica è c'aghju passatu i più belli anni di a mio giuventù.
  • Sono nato in Corsica e vi ho passato gli anni migliori della mia giovinezza.

Note that there are also regional dialects of corsican that have slightly different words.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/france for more clues.

metas.name: France - Occitan Language in France
metas.note:
Occitan is spoken in the south of France. French will still be the predominant language in this region, but you can see Occitan sometimes on street signs and even more rarely on the town sign as you enter a town.

The best hint is to note the word for "street" in the dialects spoken in Toulouse and Avignon, the two cities where it is most common to see the language (almost always close to downtown).

Toulouse - carrèira Avignon - carreiro

Note that the design you see on these street signs is also unique to their respective cities, even when they only have French.

metas.name: Italy - Italian General Tips
metas.note:
In Italian most words end in a vowel. Example exceptions include non, il, per, con, del.

  • Double consonants (tt, zz, cc, ss, bb, pp, ll, gg, etc.) are frequent.
  • Word endings: -zione, -tà, -aggio, -mento (careful spanish and portuguese use this too)
  • Letter sequences: gli, gn, sci.
  • Features of the language include: ì and à
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/italy for more clues.

metas.note:

metas.name: Portugal - Portuguese General Tips
metas.note:
Most commonly you can look for the letter ã in combination with a few other hints in order to recognize portuguese, especially words ending in -ção. Here are a few other things to look for:

  • Common two-letter words: ao, as, às, da, de, do, em, os, ou, um
  • Common three-letter words: aos, com, das, dos, ele, ela, mas, não, por, que, são, uma
  • Common endings: -ção, -dade, -ismo, -mente
  • Common digraphs: ch, nh, lh; examples: chave, galinha, baralho.

Of all the major romance languages, Spanish and Portugeuse are the two most similar sharing many words including using the word "PARE" for "STOP" in South America.

metas.name: Romania - Romanian General Tips
metas.note:
Romanian is a romance language and thus more similar to Italian/French/Spanish then to the languages of it's neighboring countries. It also uses many unique characters and patterns that make it easy to recognize with a little bit of practice.

  • ă ș ț, unique characters

  • Â â, used in French, Portuguese and Turkish

  • Î î, used in French, Turkish and Italian

  • Common words: și, de, la, a, ai, ale, alor, cu

  • Word endings: -a, -ă, -u, -ul, -ului, -ție (or -țiune), -ment, -tate;

  • names ending in -escu

  • Double and triple i: copii, copiii

Note that Romanian is sometimes written online with no diacritics, making it harder to identify. A cedilla is sometimes used on S (ş) and on T (ţ) instead of the correct diacritic, the comma (above).
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/romania for more clues.

Here are some other words similar to street in romanian: bulevard/bulevardul - avenue/boulevard piaţă - square/market calea - way intrarea - entry/entrance aleea - alley

metas.name: Spain - Aranese
metas.note:
Aranese is a language spoken only by about 2,800 people in Val d'Aran (Catalonia region of Spain west of Andorra on French border), most notably the town of Vielha. It looks very similar to Catalan and the street names are the easiest way of identifying it. Although uncommon recognizing it could give you an easy high scoring guess.

  • carrèr - (carrer in Catalan, look for the accent on the "e")
  • avenguda - (avinguda in Catalan)
  • passeg - (passeig in Catalan)

Other clues that may help you guess Val d'Aran is that it is a mountainous region with many rock buildings similar to Andorra.
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/spain for more clues.

metas.name: Spain - Basque Country Spain
metas.note:
Road signs in the Basque Country and Navarre often have these distinctive bilingual sub-signs with a thick black border. Generally you will find Basque on top in the Basque Country, while it is more common to find Spanish on top in Navarre.

Streets in Basque-speaking areas are sometimes called “kalea”. However, Spanish “calle” is also still common.

metas.name: Spain - Catalan Valencian Community
metas.note: The Valencian community in Spain also uses catalan but to a lesser extent than Catalonia. You will see more bilingual and spanish only signs but most street signs will still use the word "carrer".

metas.name: Spain - Galician
metas.note:
Galician is a romance language spoken in Spain in the area north of portugal. Unsurprisingly given it's proximity it is closely related to portuguese. In addition to the tips below the most helpful tip is to look for town names that have "A(s)" or "O(s)" in front of them ( “A Pena”, “O Burgo”, “As Cruces”). This is ALMOST unique to the galician area of Spain to see this.

  • uses ñ like spanish
  • Doesn't use ç
  • uses "nh" diagraph like portuguese but words end in -ción like spanish
  • heavier usage of the letter "x"
metas.footer: Check out www.plonkit.net/spain for more clues.

metas.name: Spain - Spanish General Tips
metas.note:
Here are some general tips to recognize Spanish:

  • Ñ is ALMOST unique to Spnaish (exception = Galician)
  • ¿ ¡ inverted question and exclamation marks are common
  • and = "y"
  • Some words frequently used: de, el, del, los, la(s), uno(s), una(s)
  • Word endings: -o, -a, -ción, -miento, -dad
  • double l "ll" more common than other romance languages (Catalan exception)
